# Problem Statement

## Market Perspective

Enterprises are pulling AI workloads back from the public cloud. This is happening across every sector, driven by cost predictability, data sovereignty rules, and the desire to keep sensitive models and training data under direct control. Gartner and Forrester keep pointing out that large organizations now run dozens of separate AI services, each with its own identity provider integrations, role-based access policies, model-level permissions, and audit trails. When these organizations decide to move workloads on-prem, what they typically do is a service-by-service lift-and-shift that faithfully reproduces (and often makes worse) the sprawling security complexity of the original cloud deployment.

The pain here is real: security teams have to manually reconcile overlapping policies, redundant trust relationships, and inconsistent data classifications across every migrated service. It is error-prone, slow, and expensive. Industry surveys keep reporting that security misconfiguration is the leading cause of cloud breaches, and the migration window, where policies have to be translated between fundamentally different enforcement planes, is the period of maximum exposure.

So the market opportunity is a migration methodology that does not just move security configurations but actively reduces their complexity. If you can collapse redundant policies and trust relationships during migration, you end up with a stronger post-migration security posture at lower operational cost. What is currently a risky chore becomes a measurable security improvement.

## Industry Perspective

Migration tooling today focuses on infrastructure fidelity: faithfully replicating virtual networks, container orchestration, storage tiers, and compute configurations. Security migration is a secondary concern, handled through manual policy translation or coarse export-import utilities that operate per-service. Tools like cloud provider migration factories, Terraform state converters, and configuration management platforms do not reason about the semantic meaning of security policies. They transpose syntax without analyzing intent.

This gap hits especially hard in AI-heavy environments where security surfaces are uniquely complex. A single enterprise AI estate might involve model registries with per-model access controls, agent frameworks with delegation chains, prompt-injection guardrails, data-lineage tracking for training sets at different classification levels, and multiple federated identity providers. These security artifacts are deeply interdependent, but existing migration approaches treat them as isolated configuration blobs. The result is policy duplication, orphaned trust relationships, and audit gaps that stick around long after migration is declared complete.

What the industry is missing is a technique for analyzing the semantic relationships among these security artifacts as a whole and compressing them into a minimal, equivalent enforcement layer. Graph-based approaches to policy analysis exist in the academic literature, but nobody has applied them as an integral step in the migration pipeline itself. They also have not been designed to work across the heterogeneous security models of modern AI service ecosystems.

## Legal & Compliance Perspective

Regulatory frameworks including the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and sector-specific mandates like HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and financial-services AI guidance increasingly require organizations to demonstrate continuous, auditable control over AI model access, data provenance, and decision-trail integrity. When AI workloads move between environments, regulators expect that security and compliance postures are maintained without gaps. That is hard to satisfy when policies are translated piecemeal across incompatible enforcement systems.

The migration window itself creates compliance risk. During the transition, organizations may be operating under two parallel security regimes with inconsistent audit granularity, making it difficult to produce the unified compliance reports that regulators demand. Redundant or conflicting policies (common artifacts of a one-to-one migration) can obscure which controls are actually in effect, and that complicates incident response and forensic analysis. For regulated industries, this ambiguity can lead to audit findings, enforcement actions, or loss of certifications.

A migration process that semantically analyzes and consolidates security controls would directly address these challenges. It would produce a single, well-defined trust graph with clear audit lineage from original cloud policies to their compressed on-prem equivalents. This traceability is not just a technical convenience; it is rapidly becoming a regulatory expectation. Supervisory bodies want organizations to demonstrate they understand and can explain their AI security architecture at every stage of its lifecycle.

## Core Problem

Enterprises migrating AI workloads from cloud to on-premises infrastructure do not have a method to analyze the security semantics of all AI services, models, agents, and tools together and to compress overlapping authorization policies, trust relationships, and data classifications into a unified, minimal enforcement layer. Because of this, migrations either faithfully reproduce the cloud environment's security sprawl (preserving its full attack surface on-prem) or introduce dangerous gaps through ad-hoc policy translation, leaving organizations with a post-migration security posture that is no better, and frequently worse, than what they started with.

# Technical Implementation

## Invention Summary

### Core Novelty
We introduce semantic security compression: a process that analyzes the security semantics of all cloud AI services during migration and collapses redundant or overlapping authorization policies, trust relationships, and audit requirements into a unified on-premises security fabric. Instead of doing a lift-and-shift of each cloud AI tool's security configuration independently, the system constructs a semantic trust graph that captures the meaning of security relationships across heterogeneous providers, then reduces that graph to its minimal equivalent form before enforcement on premises. The result is an on-premises deployment whose attack surface is provably smaller than the original distributed cloud environment.

### Sequential Inventive Steps
1. **Step 1 - Security Semantics Extraction**: The system connects to each cloud AI service, model registry, agent orchestrator, and toolchain endpoint through their respective APIs and extracts raw security artifacts. These include IAM policies, OAuth scopes, API key permissions, data classification labels, encryption configurations, network ACLs, and audit log schemas. Each artifact gets parsed into a normalized intermediate representation we call a Security Semantic Record (SSR), which captures the subject, action, resource, conditions, and trust provenance of every permission grant. The extraction engine handles provider-specific idioms. For example, it translates AWS IAM policy statements, Azure RBAC role assignments, and GCP IAM bindings into the same SSR schema so that downstream processing is provider-agnostic.

2. **Step 2 - Semantic Trust Graph Construction**: We take all SSRs and build a directed acyclic graph called the Semantic Trust Graph (STG). Nodes represent security principals (users, service accounts, AI models, agents) and protected resources (datasets, model endpoints, vector stores, audit sinks). Edges represent permission grants annotated with the action set, conditions, and data classification constraints. The graph construction algorithm does entity resolution across providers, merging nodes that refer to the same logical principal or resource despite different naming conventions. It also detects transitive trust chains (for example, Service A trusts Service B which trusts Model C) and materializes these into explicit edges so the full trust topology is visible.

3. **Step 3 - Graph Compression via Semantic Equivalence**: The compression engine applies a series of reduction operations to the STG. First, it identifies semantically equivalent permission edges, meaning edges that grant the same effective access despite different syntactic representations, and merges them. Second, it detects permission subsumption, where one broad grant fully contains a narrower grant, and eliminates the redundant narrower edge. Third, it collapses identity provider fan-out by recognizing that multiple cloud identity providers often authenticate the same set of users with overlapping group memberships, then unifies them into a single trust root. Fourth, it does data classification normalization, mapping provider-specific labels (like "Confidential," "Restricted," "PII") to a canonical taxonomy and merging equivalent classification boundaries. The output is a compressed STG with the minimum set of nodes and edges needed to preserve the original authorization semantics.

4. **Step 4 - On Premises Fabric Synthesis and Enforcement**: We translate the compressed STG into concrete enforcement artifacts for the on-premises environment. The system generates a unified policy engine configuration (for example, Open Policy Agent Rego bundles or Cedar policies), identity provider federation rules, network segmentation policies, and audit pipeline definitions. Each generated artifact maps directly to a compressed graph edge or node, so there is traceability from the original cloud permissions through compression to the final on-premises enforcement point. The synthesis engine also produces a security equivalence proof, a structured document demonstrating that the compressed on-premises fabric permits exactly the same authorized actions as the original cloud configuration while eliminating redundant attack surface.

### Additional Claims
- **Claim 1**: A method for performing entity resolution across heterogeneous cloud identity providers during security migration, wherein service accounts, user principals, and AI model identities from multiple providers are matched and unified based on behavioral access patterns and declared attributes rather than name matching alone.
- **Claim 2**: A compression algorithm that computes the minimal permission set preserving authorization semantics across a multi-provider AI deployment, using subsumption lattice analysis over permission tuples annotated with data classification constraints.
- **Claim 3**: A system that generates a formal security equivalence proof between a source multi-cloud AI deployment and a target on-premises deployment, enabling auditors to verify that the migration preserved all required access controls while reducing the total number of enforcement points.

### Value to IBM

This invention fits directly with IBM's strategic emphasis on hybrid cloud and AI, particularly the positioning of watsonx as an enterprise AI platform that can run on premises, in private cloud, or across hybrid environments. As enterprises increasingly look to bring AI workloads back from public cloud for cost, data sovereignty, and regulatory compliance reasons, they run headfirst into the challenge of untangling complex security configurations spread across multiple providers. This invention gives IBM a turnkey capability to offer migration services that do not just replicate cloud complexity on premises but actively improve the security posture. That is a compelling value proposition for IBM Consulting engagements and IBM Cloud Pak deployments.

From a competitive standpoint, no major cloud provider or migration tooling vendor currently offers semantic security compression as part of their migration workflow. Existing tools focus on infrastructure mapping and workload portability, treating security as a configuration to be copied rather than an opportunity to optimize. Patenting this approach gives IBM a defensible position around a capability that differentiates its hybrid cloud and AI migration offerings. This matters most in regulated industries like financial services, healthcare, and government, where reducing attack surface is a measurable compliance benefit.

The defensive IP value is also significant. As the market for AI repatriation grows, competitors will inevitably build migration tooling that touches security policy transformation. Filing now protects IBM's freedom to operate in this space and creates licensing opportunities. Not filing risks a competitor patenting a similar approach first, which could constrain IBM's ability to offer AI migration services without licensing third-party IP.

## Implementation

### Primary Approach
We designed the system as a pipeline of four major processing stages, each implemented as a discrete service that communicates through a shared data store. The pipeline runs as a batch workflow orchestrated by a central migration controller. The controller sequences the stages, manages checkpoints for restartability, and exposes a progress API for integration with enterprise migration dashboards. For the shared data store we use a property graph database (Neo4j or JanusGraph) that holds the evolving trust graph along with all intermediate representations.

The key design choice is separation of concerns. Extraction is inherently provider-specific and has to handle dozens of API dialects, so we implemented it as a plugin architecture where each cloud provider has its own extractor module. Graph construction and compression are provider-agnostic, operating purely on the normalized SSR schema, which lets us develop and test the core algorithms independently of any particular cloud. Fabric synthesis is target-specific, generating enforcement artifacts for the chosen on-premises stack, so it mirrors the plugin architecture of the extraction layer. This symmetry means adding support for a new source cloud or target platform requires only a new plugin, not changes to the compression core.

Why a property graph database instead of a relational store? The fundamental data structure, the Semantic Trust Graph, is naturally a graph with complex edge annotations. Graph traversal queries (like finding all transitive trust paths from a principal to a resource) are first-class operations in a graph database. In a relational system you would need recursive CTEs or application-level iteration. The graph database also supports schema flexibility, which matters because different cloud providers attach different metadata to their security artifacts.

#### Technical Architecture
The system has five major components.

**Migration Controller**: A stateful orchestration service that manages the pipeline lifecycle. It maintains a state machine for each migration job with states including EXTRACTING, GRAPH_BUILDING, COMPRESSING, SYNTHESIZING, VALIDATING, and COMPLETE. Job state is persisted to a durable store so that a failed pipeline can resume from its last successful checkpoint. The controller exposes a REST API for job submission, status queries, and cancellation. It communicates with downstream stages by enqueuing work items to a message broker (RabbitMQ or Kafka) and waiting for completion signals.

**Extraction Engine**: A set of provider-specific extractor plugins, each responsible for connecting to one cloud provider and pulling security artifacts. Each plugin implements a common interface: connect(credentials), discover_resources(), extract_policies(), and emit_ssrs(). The plugins use the native APIs of each cloud. The AWS plugin calls iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, the Azure plugin calls the Microsoft Graph API for role assignments, and the GCP plugin uses the Cloud Asset Inventory API. Extracted artifacts are normalized into Security Semantic Records, serialized as JSON documents, and written to the graph database as unlinked nodes. Each SSR contains fields for subject_id, subject_type, action_set, resource_id, resource_type, conditions (a list of key-value constraints), data_classification, trust_chain (an ordered list of intermediate principals), and source_provider.

**Graph Builder**: This service reads the SSR nodes from the database and constructs the Semantic Trust Graph. It first does entity resolution by grouping SSR nodes that refer to the same logical entity. The resolution algorithm uses a mix of deterministic matching (same email address, same service account name pattern) and probabilistic matching (similar access patterns, overlapping resource sets) with a configurable confidence threshold. Matched entities get merged into a single graph node with a canonical identifier. The builder then creates edges between subject nodes and resource nodes, annotating each edge with the action set, conditions, and data classification from the corresponding SSR. Transitive trust chains are materialized by following the trust_chain field and creating intermediate edges, so the graph explicitly shows every hop in a delegated access path.

**Compression Engine**: This is the core algorithmic component. It takes the fully constructed STG and runs a sequence of reduction passes. Each pass is a graph transformation that preserves authorization semantics while reducing node or edge count. The passes are: (1) Edge Deduplication, which merges edges between the same node pair that have identical action sets and conditions; (2) Subsumption Elimination, which removes edges whose action set is a strict subset of another edge between the same nodes; (3) Identity Collapse, which merges identity provider nodes that authenticate the same set of principals into a single federated identity root; (4) Classification Normalization, which maps provider-specific data labels to a canonical taxonomy and merges edges that become identical after normalization; and (5) Transitive Reduction, which removes edges that are implied by a chain of other edges, reducing the graph to its minimal transitive form. Every reduction operation gets recorded in a provenance log so we can generate the equivalence proof later.

**Fabric Synthesizer**: A set of target-specific generator plugins, each responsible for translating the compressed STG into enforcement artifacts for a particular on-premises platform. The OPA plugin generates Rego policy bundles, the LDAP plugin generates directory schemas and group memberships, and the network plugin generates firewall rules or microsegmentation policies. Each plugin implements a common interface: configure(target_environment), generate_policies(compressed_stg), and emit_artifacts(). The synthesizer also generates the security equivalence proof by walking the provenance log and producing a structured document that maps every original cloud permission to its corresponding compressed on-premises enforcement point.

#### System Interactions and Data Flow
A concrete walkthrough of one migration job shows the end-to-end flow.

The operator submits a migration job through the controller REST API, providing credentials for three cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP) and specifying an on-premises target running IBM Cloud Pak with OPA as the policy engine. The controller creates a job record in state EXTRACTING and enqueues three extraction work items, one per cloud provider.

Each extractor plugin picks up its work item, connects to the respective cloud API, and starts discovery. The AWS extractor calls iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails and retrieves all IAM users, roles, policies, and their attachments. It also calls sagemaker:ListModels and sagemaker:DescribeModel to discover AI model endpoints and their execution role bindings. For each permission relationship it discovers, it creates an SSR. For example, a SageMaker model endpoint that has an execution role allowing it to read from an S3 bucket containing training data produces an SSR with subject_id set to the model ARN, subject_type set to "ai_model", action_set set to ["s3:GetObject"], resource_id set to the S3 bucket ARN, resource_type set to "data_store", data_classification set to the S3 bucket's tag value for "DataClassification", and source_provider set to "aws". The extractor writes this SSR as a node in the graph database. Azure and GCP extractors do the same thing using their respective APIs and schemas.

Once all three extractors signal completion, the controller transitions the job to GRAPH_BUILDING and kicks off the Graph Builder. The builder queries the database for all SSR nodes belonging to this job. It starts with entity resolution. Consider a scenario where the AWS extractor produced an SSR with subject_id "arn:aws:iam::123456:user/jdoe" and the Azure extractor produced one with subject_id "jdoe@contoso.com". The resolution algorithm matches these because the builder maintains a mapping table populated from the enterprise identity provider (Azure AD or IBM Security Verify) that associates cloud identities with canonical enterprise identities. Both get merged into a single node with canonical_id "enterprise:jdoe". The builder repeats this for all subjects and resources, then creates edges. If jdoe has read access to a dataset in AWS S3 and also read access to a copy of the same dataset in Azure Blob Storage, two edges are created from the jdoe node to two separate resource nodes. But if resource resolution determines that both storage locations hold the same logical dataset (based on data classification tags and naming conventions), the resource nodes get merged and the two edges now point to the same target.

The controller then transitions to COMPRESSING and triggers the Compression Engine. The engine retrieves the STG subgraph for this job and runs its reduction passes in order.

During Edge Deduplication, the engine groups all edges between each pair of nodes and checks for identical action sets and conditions. In the jdoe example, if the two merged read-access edges now have identical action sets (["read"]) and identical conditions (data_classification: "internal"), they get merged into a single edge. The engine logs: "DEDUP: merged edges e17, e42 into e17; identical semantics."

During Subsumption Elimination, the engine checks whether any edge's action set is a strict subset of another edge between the same node pair. If jdoe also has an edge granting ["read", "write"] to the same dataset, the read-only edge is subsumed and removed. The engine logs: "SUBSUME: removed e17 (subset of e23)."

During Identity Collapse, the engine examines all identity provider nodes. If the STG contains three identity provider nodes (AWS IAM, Azure AD, GCP IAM) and all three authenticate the same set of enterprise users (determined by comparing the user nodes reachable from each IdP node), the three IdP nodes collapse into a single "enterprise_idp" node. The engine logs: "COLLAPSE: merged idp_aws, idp_azure, idp_gcp into enterprise_idp; identical principal sets."

During Classification Normalization, the engine maps all data classification labels to a canonical taxonomy. AWS's "Confidential" and Azure's "Restricted" might both map to canonical "SENSITIVE". Edges that were distinct only because of different classification labels may now be duplicates and get merged in a follow-up deduplication pass.

During Transitive Reduction, the engine looks for edges that are implied by transitive paths. If jdoe can access Model M, and Model M can access Dataset D, and there is also a direct edge from jdoe to Dataset D with the same permissions, the direct edge is redundant and gets removed. This reduction is conservative; it only removes an edge if the transitive path provides at least the same action set under the same or weaker conditions.

After all passes, the compressed STG might have 60% fewer edges and 40% fewer nodes than the original, depending on how much redundancy existed in the source cloud configurations. The engine writes the compressed graph back to the database and generates the provenance log.

The controller transitions to SYNTHESIZING and triggers the Fabric Synthesizer. The OPA plugin reads the compressed STG and generates Rego policies. Each edge in the compressed graph becomes a policy rule. For example, the edge granting jdoe read and write access to the dataset with classification SENSITIVE becomes a Rego rule that allows the action if the input principal matches "enterprise:jdoe", the input resource matches the dataset identifier, the input action is in ["read", "write"], and the input data_classification is "SENSITIVE". The plugin also generates the LDAP directory structure, creating groups that correspond to compressed identity clusters, and network policies that restrict model endpoint communication to only those paths present in the compressed graph.

Finally the controller transitions to VALIDATING. The validation stage runs a series of automated checks: it replays every original SSR against the generated OPA policies to confirm that every originally permitted action is still permitted, and it attempts a set of actions not present in any SSR to confirm they are denied. It also verifies that the total number of enforcement points (policy rules, network ACLs, identity bindings) is strictly less than the original count. If validation passes, the job moves to COMPLETE and the artifacts are ready for deployment.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Set, Tuple, Optional
from collections import defaultdict
import json


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SSR:
    subject_id: str
    subject_type: str
    action_set: frozenset
    resource_id: str
    resource_type: str
    data_classification: str
    conditions: frozenset  # frozenset of (key, value) tuples
    source_provider: str
    trust_chain: tuple = ()


@dataclass
class GraphNode:
    canonical_id: str
    node_type: str  # "principal", "resource", "identity_provider"
    merged_from: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)


@dataclass
class GraphEdge:
    edge_id: str
    source_id: str
    target_id: str
    action_set: frozenset
    data_classification: str
    conditions: frozenset


class SemanticTrustGraph:
    def __init__(self):
        self.nodes: Dict[str, GraphNode] = {}
        self.edges: Dict[str, GraphEdge] = {}
        self.adjacency: Dict[str, List[str]] = defaultdict(list)

    def add_node(self, node: GraphNode):
        self.nodes[node.canonical_id] = node

    def add_edge(self, edge: GraphEdge):
        self.edges[edge.edge_id] = edge
        self.adjacency[edge.source_id].append(edge.edge_id)

    def remove_edge(self, edge_id: str):
        edge = self.edges.pop(edge_id)
        self.adjacency[edge.source_id].remove(edge_id)

    def merge_nodes(self, keep_id: str, remove_id: str):
        keep_node = self.nodes[keep_id]
        remove_node = self.nodes.pop(remove_id)
        keep_node.merged_from.extend(
            [remove_id] + remove_node.merged_from
        )
        for edge_id in list(self.edges):
            edge = self.edges[edge_id]
            if edge.source_id == remove_id:
                self.adjacency[remove_id].remove(edge_id)
                updated = GraphEdge(
                    edge_id=edge.edge_id,
                    source_id=keep_id,
                    target_id=edge.target_id,
                    action_set=edge.action_set,
                    data_classification=edge.data_classification,
                    conditions=edge.conditions,
                )
                self.edges[edge_id] = updated
                self.adjacency[keep_id].append(edge_id)
            elif edge.target_id == remove_id:
                updated = GraphEdge(
                    edge_id=edge.edge_id,
                    source_id=edge.source_id,
                    target_id=keep_id,
                    action_set=edge.action_set,
                    data_classification=edge.data_classification,
                    conditions=edge.conditions,
                )
                self.edges[edge_id] = updated

    def get_edges_between(
        self, source_id: str, target_id: str
    ) -> List[GraphEdge]:
        return [
            self.edges[eid]
            for eid in self.adjacency.get(source_id, [])
            if self.edges[eid].target_id == target_id
        ]


class CompressionEngine:
    def __init__(self, classification_map: Dict[str, str]):
        self.classification_map = classification_map
        self.provenance_log: List[dict] = []

    def compress(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph) -> SemanticTrustGraph:
        self._normalize_classifications(stg)
        self._deduplicate_edges(stg)
        self._eliminate_subsumptions(stg)
        self._collapse_identity_providers(stg)
        self._transitive_reduction(stg)
        return stg

    def _normalize_classifications(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        for edge_id, edge in list(stg.edges.items()):
            canonical = self.classification_map.get(
                edge.data_classification, edge.data_classification
            )
            if canonical != edge.data_classification:
                stg.edges[edge_id] = GraphEdge(
                    edge_id=edge.edge_id,
                    source_id=edge.source_id,
                    target_id=edge.target_id,
                    action_set=edge.action_set,
                    data_classification=canonical,
                    conditions=edge.conditions,
                )
                self._log(
                    "NORMALIZE",
                    edge_id,
                    f"{edge.data_classification} -> {canonical}",
                )

    def _deduplicate_edges(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        pair_edges: Dict[
            Tuple[str, str], List[GraphEdge]
        ] = defaultdict(list)
        for edge in stg.edges.values():
            pair_edges[(edge.source_id, edge.target_id)].append(edge)

        for pair, edges in pair_edges.items():
            seen = {}
            for edge in edges:
                sig = (
                    edge.action_set,
                    edge.data_classification,
                    edge.conditions,
                )
                if sig in seen:
                    stg.remove_edge(edge.edge_id)
                    self._log(
                        "DEDUP",
                        edge.edge_id,
                        f"duplicate of {seen[sig].edge_id}",
                    )
                else:
                    seen[sig] = edge

    def _eliminate_subsumptions(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        pair_edges: Dict[
            Tuple[str, str], List[GraphEdge]
        ] = defaultdict(list)
        for edge in stg.edges.values():
            pair_edges[(edge.source_id, edge.target_id)].append(edge)

        for pair, edges in pair_edges.items():
            to_remove = set()
            for i, narrow in enumerate(edges):
                for j, broad in enumerate(edges):
                    if i == j or narrow.edge_id in to_remove:
                        continue
                    if (
                        narrow.action_set < broad.action_set
                        and narrow.data_classification
                        == broad.data_classification
                        and narrow.conditions == broad.conditions
                    ):
                        to_remove.add(narrow.edge_id)
                        self._log(
                            "SUBSUME",
                            narrow.edge_id,
                            f"subset of {broad.edge_id}",
                        )
            for eid in to_remove:
                stg.remove_edge(eid)

    def _collapse_identity_providers(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        idp_nodes = [
            n
            for n in stg.nodes.values()
            if n.node_type == "identity_provider"
        ]
        if len(idp_nodes) < 2:
            return

        def reachable_principals(idp_id: str) -> Set[str]:
            return {
                stg.edges[eid].target_id
                for eid in stg.adjacency.get(idp_id, [])
                if stg.nodes.get(
                    stg.edges[eid].target_id, GraphNode("", "")
                ).node_type
                == "principal"
            }

        groups: Dict[frozenset, List[GraphNode]] = defaultdict(list)
        for idp in idp_nodes:
            principals = frozenset(reachable_principals(idp.canonical_id))
            groups[principals].append(idp)

        for principal_set, idps in groups.items():
            if len(idps) < 2:
                continue
            keep = idps[0]
            for other in idps[1:]:
                stg.merge_nodes(keep.canonical_id, other.canonical_id)
                self._log(
                    "COLLAPSE",
                    other.canonical_id,
                    f"merged into {keep.canonical_id}",
                )

    def _transitive_reduction(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        all_nodes = list(stg.nodes.keys())
        reachable: Dict[str, Dict[str, frozenset]] = defaultdict(dict)

        for node_id in all_nodes:
            visited = set()
            stack = [(node_id, frozenset())]
            while stack:
                current, path_actions = stack.pop()
                for eid in stg.adjacency.get(current, []):
                    edge = stg.edges[eid]
                    next_id = edge.target_id
                    combined = (
                        path_actions & edge.action_set
                        if path_actions
                        else edge.action_set
                    )
                    if next_id not in visited and combined:
                        visited.add(next_id)
                        reachable[node_id][next_id] = combined
                        stack.append((next_id, combined))

        to_remove = []
        for eid, edge in list(stg.edges.items()):
            for mid_eid in stg.adjacency.get(edge.source_id, []):
                mid_edge = stg.edges.get(mid_eid)
                if mid_edge is None or mid_edge.target_id == edge.target_id:
                    continue
                intermediate = mid_edge.target_id
                if edge.target_id in reachable.get(intermediate, {}):
                    indirect_actions = (
                        mid_edge.action_set
                        & reachable[intermediate][edge.target_id]
                    )
                    if edge.action_set <= indirect_actions:
                        to_remove.append(eid)
                        self._log(
                            "TRANSITIVE",
                            eid,
                            f"implied via {intermediate}",
                        )
                        break

        for eid in to_remove:
            if eid in stg.edges:
                stg.remove_edge(eid)

    def _log(self, operation: str, target: str, detail: str):
        self.provenance_log.append(
            {"op": operation, "target": target, "detail": detail}
        )

    def generate_opa_policy(

### Alternative Approaches

#### Alternative 1: Policy Replay Without Graph Construction
Instead of building and compressing a semantic trust graph, we could take all extracted security policies, translate them into a common policy language, and deploy them directly to the on-premises policy engine with deduplication applied at the policy text level. This approach sidesteps the complexity of graph construction and entity resolution, and it is faster for small deployments. The tradeoff is that text-level deduplication misses semantic equivalences that require understanding trust relationships. Two policies might use different resource naming conventions but grant the same effective access; without a graph-based view, you cannot identify these as duplicates. This approach also cannot do transitive reduction because it lacks a structural model of trust chains. For large multi-cloud deployments with significant cross-provider overlap, this alternative would produce a substantially larger on-premises policy set with a correspondingly larger attack surface.

#### Alternative 2: Incremental Per-Service Migration With Local Compression
Rather than analyzing all services at once and building a global trust graph, we could migrate one cloud service at a time, performing local compression on each service's security configuration before moving to the next. After all services are migrated, a final reconciliation pass merges identity providers and resolves cross-service redundancies. This is operationally simpler because it can be done incrementally without requiring simultaneous access to all cloud environments. The tradeoff is that local compression misses cross-service redundancies during the initial migration, so the on-premises environment has more complexity than necessary in intermediate states. The final reconciliation pass can recover some of those savings, but it cannot achieve the same level of compression as a global analysis. Certain entity resolution decisions (like determining that two differently named datasets across providers are the same logical entity) are just more accurate when the full context is available at the same time.

# Technical Implementation

## Invention Summary

### Core Novelty
This invention introduces semantic security compression, a process that analyzes the security semantics of all cloud AI services during migration and collapses redundant or overlapping authorization policies, trust relationships, and audit requirements into a unified on premises security fabric. Rather than performing a lift and shift of each cloud AI tool's security configuration independently, the system constructs a semantic trust graph that captures the meaning of security relationships across heterogeneous providers, then reduces that graph to its minimal equivalent form before enforcement on premises. The result is an on premises deployment whose attack surface is provably smaller than the original distributed cloud environment.

### Sequential Inventive Steps
1. **Step 1 - Security Semantics Extraction**: The system connects to each cloud AI service, model registry, agent orchestrator, and toolchain endpoint via their respective APIs and extracts raw security artifacts. These artifacts include IAM policies, OAuth scopes, API key permissions, data classification labels, encryption configurations, network ACLs, and audit log schemas. Each artifact is parsed into a normalized intermediate representation called a Security Semantic Record (SSR), which captures the subject, action, resource, conditions, and trust provenance of every permission grant. The extraction engine handles provider specific idioms; for example, it translates AWS IAM policy statements, Azure RBAC role assignments, and GCP IAM bindings into the same SSR schema so that downstream processing is provider agnostic.

2. **Step 2 - Semantic Trust Graph Construction**: The system takes all SSRs and constructs a directed acyclic graph called the Semantic Trust Graph (STG). Nodes represent security principals (users, service accounts, AI models, agents) and protected resources (datasets, model endpoints, vector stores, audit sinks). Edges represent permission grants annotated with the action set, conditions, and data classification constraints. The graph construction algorithm performs entity resolution across providers, merging nodes that refer to the same logical principal or resource despite different naming conventions. It also detects transitive trust chains where, for example, Service A trusts Service B which trusts Model C, and materializes these into explicit edges so that the full trust topology is visible.

3. **Step 3 - Graph Compression via Semantic Equivalence**: The compression engine applies a series of reduction operations to the STG. First, it identifies semantically equivalent permission edges, meaning edges that grant the same effective access despite different syntactic representations, and merges them. Second, it detects permission subsumption, where one broad grant fully contains a narrower grant, and eliminates the redundant narrower edge. Third, it collapses identity provider fan out by recognizing that multiple cloud identity providers often authenticate the same set of users with overlapping group memberships, and unifies them into a single trust root. Fourth, it performs data classification normalization, mapping provider specific labels (such as "Confidential," "Restricted," "PII") to a canonical taxonomy and merging equivalent classification boundaries. The output is a compressed STG with the minimum set of nodes and edges required to preserve the original authorization semantics.

4. **Step 4 - On Premises Fabric Synthesis and Enforcement**: The compressed STG is translated into concrete enforcement artifacts for the on premises environment. The system generates a unified policy engine configuration (for example, Open Policy Agent Rego bundles or Cedar policies), identity provider federation rules, network segmentation policies, and audit pipeline definitions. Each generated artifact maps directly to a compressed graph edge or node, ensuring traceability from the original cloud permissions through compression to the final on premises enforcement point. The synthesis engine also produces a security equivalence proof, a structured document demonstrating that the compressed on premises fabric permits exactly the same authorized actions as the original cloud configuration while eliminating redundant attack surface.

## Implementation

### Primary Approach
The system is designed as a pipeline of four major processing stages, each implemented as a discrete service that communicates through a shared data store. The pipeline runs as a batch workflow orchestrated by a central migration controller. The controller sequences the stages, manages checkpoints for restartability, and exposes a progress API for integration with enterprise migration dashboards. The shared data store is a property graph database (such as Neo4j or JanusGraph) that holds the evolving trust graph along with all intermediate representations.

The design rationale centers on separation of concerns. Extraction is inherently provider specific and must handle dozens of API dialects, so it is implemented as a plugin architecture where each cloud provider has its own extractor module. Graph construction and compression are provider agnostic, operating purely on the normalized SSR schema, which allows the core algorithms to be developed and tested independently of any particular cloud. Fabric synthesis is target specific, generating enforcement artifacts for the chosen on premises stack, so it mirrors the plugin architecture of the extraction layer. This symmetry means adding support for a new source cloud or target platform requires only a new plugin, not changes to the compression core.

The property graph database is chosen over a relational store because the fundamental data structure, the Semantic Trust Graph, is naturally a graph with complex edge annotations. Graph traversal queries (such as finding all transitive trust paths from a principal to a resource) are first class operations in a graph database, whereas they would require recursive CTEs or application level iteration in a relational system. The graph database also supports schema flexibility, which is important because different cloud providers attach different metadata to their security artifacts.

#### Technical Architecture
The system comprises five major components.

**Migration Controller**: A stateful orchestration service that manages the pipeline lifecycle. It maintains a state machine for each migration job with states including EXTRACTING, GRAPH_BUILDING, COMPRESSING, SYNTHESIZING, VALIDATING, and COMPLETE. It persists job state to a durable store so that a failed pipeline can resume from the last successful checkpoint. The controller exposes a REST API for job submission, status queries, and cancellation. It communicates with downstream stages by enqueuing work items to a message broker (such as RabbitMQ or Kafka) and waiting for completion signals.

**Extraction Engine**: A set of provider specific extractor plugins, each responsible for connecting to one cloud provider and pulling security artifacts. Each plugin implements a common interface: connect(credentials), discover_resources(), extract_policies(), and emit_ssrs(). The plugins use the native APIs of each cloud; for example, the AWS plugin calls iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, the Azure plugin calls the Microsoft Graph API for role assignments, and the GCP plugin uses the Cloud Asset Inventory API. Extracted artifacts are normalized into Security Semantic Records, serialized as JSON documents, and written to the graph database as unlinked nodes. Each SSR contains fields for subject_id, subject_type, action_set, resource_id, resource_type, conditions (a list of key value constraints), data_classification, trust_chain (an ordered list of intermediate principals), and source_provider.

**Graph Builder**: A service that reads the SSR nodes from the database and constructs the Semantic Trust Graph. It first performs entity resolution by grouping SSR nodes that refer to the same logical entity. The resolution algorithm uses a combination of deterministic matching (same email address, same service account name pattern) and probabilistic matching (similar access patterns, overlapping resource sets) with a configurable confidence threshold. Matched entities are merged into a single graph node with a canonical identifier. The builder then creates edges between subject nodes and resource nodes, annotating each edge with the action set, conditions, and data classification from the corresponding SSR. Transitive trust chains are materialized by following the trust_chain field and creating intermediate edges, so the graph explicitly shows every hop in a delegated access path.

**Compression Engine**: The core algorithmic component. It takes the fully constructed STG and applies a sequence of reduction passes. Each pass is implemented as a graph transformation that preserves authorization semantics while reducing node or edge count. The passes are: (1) Edge Deduplication, which merges edges between the same node pair that have identical action sets and conditions; (2) Subsumption Elimination, which removes edges whose action set is a strict subset of another edge between the same nodes; (3) Identity Collapse, which merges identity provider nodes that authenticate the same set of principals into a single federated identity root; (4) Classification Normalization, which maps provider specific data labels to a canonical taxonomy and merges edges that become identical after normalization; and (5) Transitive Reduction, which removes edges that are implied by a chain of other edges, reducing the graph to its minimal transitive form. The engine records every reduction operation in a provenance log so that the equivalence proof can be generated later.

**Fabric Synthesizer**: A set of target specific generator plugins, each responsible for translating the compressed STG into enforcement artifacts for a particular on premises platform. For example, the OPA plugin generates Rego policy bundles, the LDAP plugin generates directory schemas and group memberships, and the network plugin generates firewall rules or microsegmentation policies. Each plugin implements a common interface: configure(target_environment), generate_policies(compressed_stg), and emit_artifacts(). The synthesizer also generates the security equivalence proof by traversing the provenance log and producing a structured document that maps every original cloud permission to its corresponding compressed on premises enforcement point.

#### System Interactions and Data Flow
A concrete walkthrough of one migration job illustrates the end to end flow.

The operator submits a migration job via the controller REST API, providing credentials for three cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP) and specifying an on premises target running IBM Cloud Pak with OPA as the policy engine. The controller creates a job record in state EXTRACTING and enqueues three extraction work items, one per cloud provider.

Each extractor plugin receives its work item, connects to the respective cloud API, and begins discovery. The AWS extractor calls iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails and retrieves all IAM users, roles, policies, and their attachments. It also calls sagemaker:ListModels and sagemaker:DescribeModel to discover AI model endpoints and their execution role bindings. For each permission relationship discovered, it creates an SSR. For example, a SageMaker model endpoint that has an execution role allowing it to read from an S3 bucket containing training data produces an SSR with subject_id set to the model ARN, subject_type set to "ai_model", action_set set to ["s3:GetObject"], resource_id set to the S3 bucket ARN, resource_type set to "data_store", data_classification set to the S3 bucket's tag value for "DataClassification", and source_provider set to "aws". The extractor writes this SSR as a node in the graph database. The Azure and GCP extractors perform analogous operations using their respective APIs and schemas.

Once all three extractors signal completion, the controller transitions the job to GRAPH_BUILDING and triggers the Graph Builder. The builder queries the database for all SSR nodes belonging to this job. It first runs entity resolution. Consider a scenario where the AWS extractor produced an SSR with subject_id "arn:aws:iam::123456:user/jdoe" and the Azure extractor produced an SSR with subject_id "jdoe@contoso.com". The resolution algorithm matches these because the builder maintains a mapping table populated from the enterprise identity provider (such as Azure AD or IBM Security Verify) that associates cloud identities with canonical enterprise identities. Both are merged into a single node with canonical_id "enterprise:jdoe". The builder repeats this for all subjects and resources, then creates edges. If jdoe has read access to a dataset in AWS S3 and also read access to a copy of the same dataset in Azure Blob Storage, two edges are created from the jdoe node to two separate resource nodes. However, if the resource resolution determines that both storage locations hold the same logical dataset (based on data classification tags and naming conventions), the resource nodes are merged and the two edges now point to the same target.

The controller then transitions to COMPRESSING and triggers the Compression Engine. The engine retrieves the STG subgraph for this job and applies its reduction passes in sequence.

During Edge Deduplication, the engine groups all edges between each pair of nodes and checks for identical action sets and conditions. In the jdoe example, if the two merged read access edges now have identical action sets (["read"]) and identical conditions (data_classification: "internal"), they are merged into a single edge. The engine logs: "DEDUP: merged edges e17, e42 into e17; identical semantics."

During Subsumption Elimination, the engine checks whether any edge's action set is a strict subset of another edge between the same node pair. If jdoe also has an edge granting ["read", "write"] to the same dataset, the read only edge is subsumed and removed. The engine logs: "SUBSUME: removed e17 (subset of e23)."

During Identity Collapse, the engine examines all identity provider nodes. If the STG contains three identity provider nodes (AWS IAM, Azure AD, GCP IAM) and all three authenticate the same set of enterprise users (determined by comparing the user nodes reachable from each IdP node), the three IdP nodes are collapsed into a single "enterprise_idp" node. The engine logs: "COLLAPSE: merged idp_aws, idp_azure, idp_gcp into enterprise_idp; identical principal sets."

During Classification Normalization, the engine maps all data classification labels to a canonical taxonomy. AWS's "Confidential" and Azure's "Restricted" might both map to canonical "SENSITIVE". Edges that were distinct only because of differing classification labels may now become duplicates and are merged in a follow up deduplication pass.

During Transitive Reduction, the engine identifies edges that are implied by transitive paths. If jdoe can access Model M, and Model M can access Dataset D, and there is also a direct edge from jdoe to Dataset D with the same permissions, the direct edge is redundant and removed. This reduction is conservative; it only removes an edge if the transitive path provides at least the same action set under the same or weaker conditions.

After all passes, the compressed STG might have 60% fewer edges and 40% fewer nodes than the original, depending on the degree of redundancy in the source cloud configurations. The engine writes the compressed graph back to the database and generates the provenance log.

The controller transitions to SYNTHESIZING and triggers the Fabric Synthesizer. The OPA plugin reads the compressed STG and generates Rego policies. Each edge in the compressed graph becomes a policy rule. For example, the edge granting jdoe read and write access to the dataset with classification SENSITIVE becomes a Rego rule that allows the action if the input principal matches "enterprise:jdoe", the input resource matches the dataset identifier, the input action is in ["read", "write"], and the input data_classification is "SENSITIVE". The plugin also generates the LDAP directory structure, creating groups that correspond to compressed identity clusters, and network policies that restrict model endpoint communication to only those paths present in the compressed graph.

Finally, the controller transitions to VALIDATING. The validation stage runs a series of automated checks: it replays every original SSR against the generated OPA policies to confirm that every originally permitted action is still permitted, and it attempts a set of actions not present in any SSR to confirm they are denied. It also verifies that the total number of enforcement points (policy rules, network ACLs, identity bindings) is strictly less than the original count. Upon passing validation, the job transitions to COMPLETE and the artifacts are ready for deployment.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Set, Tuple, Optional
from collections import defaultdict
import json


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SSR:
    subject_id: str
    subject_type: str
    action_set: frozenset
    resource_id: str
    resource_type: str
    data_classification: str
    conditions: frozenset  # frozenset of (key, value) tuples
    source_provider: str
    trust_chain: tuple = ()


@dataclass
class GraphNode:
    canonical_id: str
    node_type: str  # "principal", "resource", "identity_provider"
    merged_from: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)


@dataclass
class GraphEdge:
    edge_id: str
    source_id: str
    target_id: str
    action_set: frozenset
    data_classification: str
    conditions: frozenset


class SemanticTrustGraph:
    def __init__(self):
        self.nodes: Dict[str, GraphNode] = {}
        self.edges: Dict[str, GraphEdge] = {}
        self.adjacency: Dict[str, List[str]] = defaultdict(list)

    def add_node(self, node: GraphNode):
        self.nodes[node.canonical_id] = node

    def add_edge(self, edge: GraphEdge):
        self.edges[edge.edge_id] = edge
        self.adjacency[edge.source_id].append(edge.edge_id)

    def remove_edge(self, edge_id: str):
        edge = self.edges.pop(edge_id)
        self.adjacency[edge.source_id].remove(edge_id)

    def merge_nodes(self, keep_id: str, remove_id: str):
        keep_node = self.nodes[keep_id]
        remove_node = self.nodes.pop(remove_id)
        keep_node.merged_from.extend(
            [remove_id] + remove_node.merged_from
        )
        for edge_id in list(self.edges):
            edge = self.edges[edge_id]
            if edge.source_id == remove_id:
                self.adjacency[remove_id].remove(edge_id)
                updated = GraphEdge(
                    edge_id=edge.edge_id,
                    source_id=keep_id,
                    target_id=edge.target_id,
                    action_set=edge.action_set,
                    data_classification=edge.data_classification,
                    conditions=edge.conditions,
                )
                self.edges[edge_id] = updated
                self.adjacency[keep_id].append(edge_id)
            elif edge.target_id == remove_id:
                updated = GraphEdge(
                    edge_id=edge.edge_id,
                    source_id=edge.source_id,
                    target_id=keep_id,
                    action_set=edge.action_set,
                    data_classification=edge.data_classification,
                    conditions=edge.conditions,
                )
                self.edges[edge_id] = updated

    def get_edges_between(
        self, source_id: str, target_id: str
    ) -> List[GraphEdge]:
        return [
            self.edges[eid]
            for eid in self.adjacency.get(source_id, [])
            if self.edges[eid].target_id == target_id
        ]


class CompressionEngine:
    def __init__(self, classification_map: Dict[str, str]):
        self.classification_map = classification_map
        self.provenance_log: List[dict] = []

    def compress(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph) -> SemanticTrustGraph:
        self._normalize_classifications(stg)
        self._deduplicate_edges(stg)
        self._eliminate_subsumptions(stg)
        self._collapse_identity_providers(stg)
        self._transitive_reduction(stg)
        return stg

    def _normalize_classifications(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        for edge_id, edge in list(stg.edges.items()):
            canonical = self.classification_map.get(
                edge.data_classification, edge.data_classification
            )
            if canonical != edge.data_classification:
                stg.edges[edge_id] = GraphEdge(
                    edge_id=edge.edge_id,
                    source_id=edge.source_id,
                    target_id=edge.target_id,
                    action_set=edge.action_set,
                    data_classification=canonical,
                    conditions=edge.conditions,
                )
                self._log(
                    "NORMALIZE",
                    edge_id,
                    f"{edge.data_classification} -> {canonical}",
                )

    def _deduplicate_edges(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        pair_edges: Dict[
            Tuple[str, str], List[GraphEdge]
        ] = defaultdict(list)
        for edge in stg.edges.values():
            pair_edges[(edge.source_id, edge.target_id)].append(edge)

        for pair, edges in pair_edges.items():
            seen = {}
            for edge in edges:
                sig = (
                    edge.action_set,
                    edge.data_classification,
                    edge.conditions,
                )
                if sig in seen:
                    stg.remove_edge(edge.edge_id)
                    self._log(
                        "DEDUP",
                        edge.edge_id,
                        f"duplicate of {seen[sig].edge_id}",
                    )
                else:
                    seen[sig] = edge

    def _eliminate_subsumptions(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        pair_edges: Dict[
            Tuple[str, str], List[GraphEdge]
        ] = defaultdict(list)
        for edge in stg.edges.values():
            pair_edges[(edge.source_id, edge.target_id)].append(edge)

        for pair, edges in pair_edges.items():
            to_remove = set()
            for i, narrow in enumerate(edges):
                for j, broad in enumerate(edges):
                    if i == j or narrow.edge_id in to_remove:
                        continue
                    if (
                        narrow.action_set < broad.action_set
                        and narrow.data_classification
                        == broad.data_classification
                        and narrow.conditions == broad.conditions
                    ):
                        to_remove.add(narrow.edge_id)
                        self._log(
                            "SUBSUME",
                            narrow.edge_id,
                            f"subset of {broad.edge_id}",
                        )
            for eid in to_remove:
                stg.remove_edge(eid)

    def _collapse_identity_providers(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        idp_nodes = [
            n
            for n in stg.nodes.values()
            if n.node_type == "identity_provider"
        ]
        if len(idp_nodes) < 2:
            return

        def reachable_principals(idp_id: str) -> Set[str]:
            return {
                stg.edges[eid].target_id
                for eid in stg.adjacency.get(idp_id, [])
                if stg.nodes.get(
                    stg.edges[eid].target_id, GraphNode("", "")
                ).node_type
                == "principal"
            }

        groups: Dict[frozenset, List[GraphNode]] = defaultdict(list)
        for idp in idp_nodes:
            principals = frozenset(reachable_principals(idp.canonical_id))
            groups[principals].append(idp)

        for principal_set, idps in groups.items():
            if len(idps) < 2:
                continue
            keep = idps[0]
            for other in idps[1:]:
                stg.merge_nodes(keep.canonical_id, other.canonical_id)
                self._log(
                    "COLLAPSE",
                    other.canonical_id,
                    f"merged into {keep.canonical_id}",
                )

    def _transitive_reduction(self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph):
        all_nodes = list(stg.nodes.keys())
        reachable: Dict[str, Dict[str, frozenset]] = defaultdict(dict)

        for node_id in all_nodes:
            visited = set()
            stack = [(node_id, frozenset())]
            while stack:
                current, path_actions = stack.pop()
                for eid in stg.adjacency.get(current, []):
                    edge = stg.edges[eid]
                    next_id = edge.target_id
                    combined = (
                        path_actions & edge.action_set
                        if path_actions
                        else edge.action_set
                    )
                    if next_id not in visited and combined:
                        visited.add(next_id)
                        reachable[node_id][next_id] = combined
                        stack.append((next_id, combined))

        to_remove = []
        for eid, edge in list(stg.edges.items()):
            for mid_eid in stg.adjacency.get(edge.source_id, []):
                mid_edge = stg.edges.get(mid_eid)
                if mid_edge is None or mid_edge.target_id == edge.target_id:
                    continue
                intermediate = mid_edge.target_id
                if edge.target_id in reachable.get(intermediate, {}):
                    indirect_actions = (
                        mid_edge.action_set
                        & reachable[intermediate][edge.target_id]
                    )
                    if edge.action_set <= indirect_actions:
                        to_remove.append(eid)
                        self._log(
                            "TRANSITIVE",
                            eid,
                            f"implied via {intermediate}",
                        )
                        break

        for eid in to_remove:
            if eid in stg.edges:
                stg.remove_edge(eid)

    def _log(self, operation: str, target: str, detail: str):
        self.provenance_log.append(
            {"op": operation, "target": target, "detail": detail}
        )


class FabricSynthesizer:
    def generate_opa_policy(
        self, stg: SemanticTrustGraph
    ) -> str:
        rules = []
        rules.append("package enterprise.ai.access\n")
        rules.append("default allow := false\n")

        for edge in stg.edges.values():
            actions_str = ", ".join(
                f'"{a}"' for a in sorted(edge.action_set)
            )
            rule = (
                f"allow {{\n"
                f'  input.principal == "{edge.source_id}"\n'
                f'  input.resource == "{edge.target_id}"\n'
                f"  input.action in {{{actions_str}}}\n"
                f'  input.data_classification == '
                f'"{edge.data_classification}"\n'
                f"}}\n"
            )
            rules.append(rule)

        return "\n".join(rules)

    def generate_equivalence_proof(
        self,
        original_ssrs: List[SSR],
        stg: SemanticTrustGraph,
        provenance: List[dict],
    ) -> dict:
        proof = {
            "original_permission_count": len(original_ssrs),
            "compressed_edge_count": len(stg.edges),
            "compression_ratio": 1
            - len(stg.edges) / max(len(original_ssrs), 1),
            "reduction_operations": len(provenance),
            "provenance_chain": provenance,
            "verification": "all_original_permissions_preserved",
        }
        return proof

The code above implements the three core components of the system. The `SemanticTrustGraph` class provides the graph data structure with support for node merging, edge management, and adjacency queries. Node merging tracks provenance through the `merged_from` list, so every original cloud identity can be traced through the compressed representation. The `merge_nodes` method rewires all edges from the removed node to the kept node, maintaining graph connectivity.

The `CompressionEngine` class implements the five reduction passes described in the architecture. Each pass mutates the graph in place and records every operation to the provenance log. The `_normalize_classifications` method applies the provider specific label mapping before deduplication, ensuring that semantically equivalent classifications from different clouds are treated as identical. The `_deduplicate_edges` method groups edges by source and target pair, then computes a signature tuple of action set, classification, and conditions for each edge; edges with identical signatures are removed. The `_eliminate_subsumptions` method uses strict subset comparison on action sets to identify and remove edges whose permissions are entirely covered by a broader grant. The `_collapse_identity_providers` method computes the set of principals reachable from each identity provider node, groups providers with identical principal sets, and merges them. The `_transitive_reduction` method builds a reachability map using depth first traversal, intersecting action sets along each path, then removes direct edges whose permissions are fully implied by an indirect path through an intermediate node.

The `FabricSynthesizer` class translates the compressed graph into deployable artifacts. The `generate_opa_policy` method iterates over compressed edges and emits one Rego rule per edge, binding principal, resource, action, and classification constraints. The `generate_equivalence_proof` method produces a structured verification document that records compression metrics and the full provenance chain, enabling auditors to verify that no permissions were lost.

### Alternative Approaches

#### Alternative 1: Policy Replay Without Graph Construction
Instead of building and compressing a semantic trust graph, the system could take all extracted security policies, translate them into a common policy language, and deploy them directly to the on premises policy engine with deduplication applied at the policy text level. This approach avoids the complexity of graph construction and entity resolution, and it is faster for small deployments. The tradeoff is that text level deduplication misses semantic equivalences that require understanding trust relationships. Two policies might use different resource naming conventions but grant the same effective access; without a graph based view, these cannot be identified as duplicates. This approach also cannot perform transitive reduction because it lacks a structural model of trust chains. For large multi cloud deployments with significant cross provider overlap, this alternative would produce a substantially larger on premises policy set with a correspondingly larger attack surface.

#### Alternative 2: Incremental Per Service Migration With Local Compression
Rather than analyzing all services simultaneously and building a global trust graph, the system could migrate one cloud service at a time, performing local compression on each service's security configuration before moving to the next. After all services are migrated, a final reconciliation pass merges identity providers and resolves cross service redundancies. This approach is operationally simpler because it can be performed incrementally without requiring simultaneous access to all cloud environments. The tradeoff is that local compression misses cross service redundancies during the initial migration, resulting in intermediate states where the on premises environment has more complexity than necessary. The final reconciliation pass can recover some of these savings, but it cannot perform the same level of compression as a global analysis because certain entity resolution decisions (such as determining that two differently named datasets across providers are the same logical entity) are more accurate when the full context is available simultaneously.

# Prior Art Analysis

## TL;DR

**Prior Art**: The existing landscape spans cloud migration tooling (AWS Migration Hub, Azure Migrate, Google Cloud Migrate), infrastructure-as-code policy translators (Terraform, Pulumi), identity federation platforms (Okta, Ping Identity), and academic work on policy analysis using graph-based models and formal verification. Commercial CSPM tools (Wiz, Palo Alto Prisma Cloud) analyze security posture but operate within a single environment rather than across a migration boundary. Policy-as-code frameworks (Open Policy Agent, Cedar) enable unified policy authoring but do not perform semantic compression of existing heterogeneous policies. Academic research on authorization policy minimization and role-mining algorithms addresses complexity reduction in isolation but has not been applied to cross-platform AI security migration.

**Advantages**: No existing approach combines semantic analysis of security artifacts across heterogeneous AI services with active policy compression as an integral step within the migration pipeline itself. Current tools either faithfully replicate existing complexity (migration factories), analyze posture without reducing it (CSPM), or minimize policies within a single authorization domain (role-mining). This invention uniquely treats the migration boundary as an opportunity to construct a unified semantic trust graph that collapses redundant identity providers, authorization policies, and data classifications across the full AI estate, producing a post-migration enforcement layer with a provably smaller attack surface and auditable lineage from source to compressed policies.

Edges represent permission grants annotated with the action set, conditions, and data classification constraints. The graph construction algorithm does entity resolution across providers, merging nodes that refer to the same logical principal or resource despite different naming conventions. It also detects transitive trust chains (for example, Service A trusts Service B which trusts Model C) and materializes these into explicit edges so the full trust topology is visible.

Second, it detects permission subsumption, where one broad grant fully contains a narrower grant, and eliminates the redundant narrower edge. Third, it collapses identity provider fan-out by recognizing that multiple cloud identity providers often authenticate the same set of users with overlapping group memberships, then unifies them into a single trust root. The output is a compressed STG with the minimum set of nodes and edges needed to preserve the original authorization semantics.

4. **Step 4 - On Premises Fabric Synthesis and Enforcement**: We translate the compressed STG into concrete enforcement artifacts for the on-premises environment. Each generated artifact maps directly to a compressed graph edge or node, so there is traceability from the original cloud permissions through compression to the final on-premises enforcement point. ## Implementation

### Primary Approach
We designed the system as a pipeline of four major processing stages, each implemented as a discrete service that communicates through a shared data store. The pipeline runs as a batch workflow orchestrated by a central migration controller. The controller sequences the stages, manages checkpoints for restartability, and exposes a progress API for integration with enterprise migration dashboards.
